The core idea of relevance-based prediction hinges on modeling draft prospects using Mahalanobis distances to account for correlations among predictive variables. Each previously drafted player contributes to the prediction through a relevance weight derived from their similarity to the draft prospect, adjusted by the inverse covariance matrix. This formulation allows for a principled way to incorporate multivariate dependencies without assuming independence. The relevance-weighted average of outcomes mirrors linear regression under certain conditions, providing theoretical grounding. Information alignment further refines this by incorporating outcome data into the relevance computation, yielding a measure of fit that quantifies how reliably a prediction task can be executed. These primitives form a dual framework: one rooted in geometric similarity (Mahalanobis), and another in statistical alignment (information). Failure modes include rank deficiency in the covariance matrix, leading to unstable relevance estimates, and poor outcome alignment indicating unreliable predictions.
